lessonTitle: Boundary Work: Energy Transfer by Expansion and Compression

blocks.text: A bicycle pump gets warm and gets harder to push as the piston moves in. The force you feel is the gas pressure acting on the piston face, and the energy you supply is boundary work, the subject of this unit.

blocks.markdown: When a gas in a piston-cylinder device pushes the piston outward by a small distance $dx$, the force on the piston is $pA$ and the work is $pA\,dx = p\,dV$, where $p$ is the absolute gas pressure (Pa), $A$ the piston area (m$^2$) and $dV$ the volume change (m$^3$). Adding up these small pieces along the whole process gives the **boundary work**. It exists only while the boundary moves, so a rigid tank has none.

blocks.title: Boundary work and sign convention
blocks.text: Boundary work is the work done by or on a closed system through the motion of its boundary. In this course the sign convention is: work done BY the system is positive (expansion, dV > 0); work done ON the system is negative (compression, dV < 0). Some texts use the opposite convention, so always state which one you are using.

blocks.caption: Boundary work for a quasi-equilibrium process; the integral needs p as a function of V, that is, the process path

blocks.markdown: The integral is the **area under the process curve on a $p$-$V$ diagram**. Two different paths between the same end states enclose different areas, so boundary work depends on the path and is not a property of the states. Expansion moves right on the diagram (positive area, positive work); compression moves left (negative work).

blocks.caption: The common quasi-equilibrium processes; polytropic with n = 0 is isobaric, n = 1 is isothermal for an ideal gas, and n tending to infinity is constant volume

blocks.title: Isobaric expansion
blocks.prompt: A gas at a constant absolute pressure of 200 kPa expands in a piston-cylinder from 0.10 m$^3$ to 0.35 m$^3$. Find the boundary work done by the gas.

steps.text: Pressure is constant, so it comes out of the integral.
Substitute with consistent units (kPa times m$^3$ gives kJ).

blocks.answer: W_b = 50 kJ, positive because the gas expands and does work on its surroundings.

blocks.markdown: For polytropic processes the pressure falls as $p=C/V^n$ with $C=p_1V_1^n=p_2V_2^n$. Integrating gives the table result for $n\ne 1$. For $n=1$ the integral of $C/V$ gives a logarithm. Both only apply to quasi-equilibrium paths where the pressure is uniform throughout the gas.

blocks.title: Polytropic expansion
blocks.prompt: A gas expands from 600 kPa and 0.02 m$^3$ to 0.08 m$^3$ following $pV^{1.3}=\text{constant}$. Find the final pressure and the boundary work.

steps.text: Use the path law to find the final pressure.

blocks.answer: p2 is about 99.0 kPa and W_b is about 13.6 kJ (positive, expansion).

items: Write the pressure as a function of volume for the stated path.
Check the sign: right-moving on the p-V diagram is positive work by the system.
Use absolute pressure, never gauge, in the integral for a closed gas.
Convert units so that kPa times m$^3$ gives kJ.

blocks.title: Gauge pressure and the atmosphere
blocks.text: The work done by the gas uses the gas absolute pressure. If part of the work only pushes back the atmosphere, that part is real work but is not useful output; do not confuse the two.

blocks.title: Area and path
blocks.text: Boundary work equals the area under the p-V path. A closed cycle that runs clockwise on a p-V diagram has positive net work equal to the enclosed area; anticlockwise gives negative net work.

points: Boundary work is the integral of p dV along the actual process path and needs p(V).
Use W = p(V2 - V1) for isobaric, p1V1 ln(V2/V1) for isothermal ideal gas, and (p2V2 - p1V1)/(1 - n) for polytropic with n not 1.
Work by the system is positive on expansion and negative on compression, with the sign convention stated.
The magnitude is the area under the curve on a p-V diagram, which is why path matters.

questions.stem: Using the convention that work done by the system is positive, a gas in a cylinder is compressed from 0.30 m$^3$ to 0.10 m$^3$. What is the sign of the boundary work?

options.text: Negative, because dV < 0 so work is done on the gas
Positive, because pressure is always positive
Zero, because the process ends in a closed system
Positive, because the gas gains energy

questions.correctOptionText: Negative, because dV < 0 so work is done on the gas

distractorRationale.b: Pressure positive does not fix the sign; dV does.
distractorRationale.c: Closed systems can exchange boundary work.
distractorRationale.d: Energy gain by the gas means work done ON it, which is negative here.

questions.explanation: The sign of boundary work follows the sign of dV because p is always positive. Compression makes dV negative, so work done by the gas is negative, meaning energy is supplied to the gas.

questions.stem: On a p-V diagram a gas follows a clockwise closed loop returning to its initial state. Which statement about the net boundary work over the loop is correct?

options.text: It is zero because the end state equals the start state
It is positive and equals the area enclosed by the loop
It is negative and equals the area enclosed by the loop
It equals the change in internal energy

questions.correctOptionText: It is positive and equals the area enclosed by the loop

distractorRationale.a: Work is path dependent, so a cycle need not give zero.
distractorRationale.d: The internal energy change over a cycle is zero, not the work.

questions.explanation: Going clockwise, the expansion occurs at higher pressure than the compression, so the area under the upper path exceeds the area under the lower path. The net boundary work by the gas is therefore positive and equals the enclosed area.

questions.stem: For a polytropic process $pV^n=\text{constant}$, which value of $n$ gives a constant-pressure (isobaric) process?

options.text: n tending to infinity

distractorRationale.a: That is isothermal for an ideal gas.
distractorRationale.c: That is a typical air isentropic index, not isobaric.

questions.explanation: With n = 0 the law becomes p = constant. The values n = 1 and n tending to infinity give pV = constant and constant volume respectively.

questions.stem: Air at the same initial state is compressed to half its volume, once isothermally and once along $pV^{1.4}=\text{constant}$. Which statement about the magnitude of the boundary work is correct?

options.text: The two are equal because the end volumes are equal
The isothermal compression needs more work because the temperature stays low
The n = 1.4 compression needs more work because pressure rises faster, giving a larger area under the curve
Neither needs work because the system is closed

questions.correctOptionText: The n = 1.4 compression needs more work because pressure rises faster, giving a larger area under the curve

distractorRationale.a: Work depends on path, not only on end volumes.
distractorRationale.b: Constant temperature keeps the pressure lower, which means less area.
distractorRationale.d: Boundary work occurs in closed systems.

questions.explanation: Along pV^1.4 = constant the pressure at every volume is higher than on the isothermal curve, so the area under the compression path is larger. A higher pressure means more work is required to push the same volume change.

questions.stem: A gas expands with pressure falling linearly from 400 kPa at 0.01 m$^3$ to 100 kPa at 0.05 m$^3$. What is the boundary work done by the gas?

options.text: 16 kJ
10 kJ
4 kJ
20 kJ

distractorRationale.a: Uses the starting pressure over the whole volume change.
distractorRationale.c: Uses the final pressure over the whole volume change.
distractorRationale.d: Adds the two pressures instead of averaging them.

questions.explanation: The path is a straight line, so the area under it is a trapezoid: mean pressure (400+100)/2 = 250 kPa times a volume change of 0.04 m^3 gives 10 kJ. Using one end pressure only gives an upper or lower bound.

questions.stem: A gas is compressed at a constant absolute pressure of 150 kPa from 0.40 m$^3$ to 0.15 m$^3$. Using the sign convention that work by the system is positive, find the boundary work in kJ.
questions.explanation: Isobaric work is W = p(V2 - V1) = 150 x (0.15 - 0.40) = -37.50 kJ. The negative sign shows that work is done on the gas during compression.

questions.stem: A cylinder holds 0.20 kg of air (treat as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K)) at 300 K. It is compressed isothermally to one third of its initial volume. Find the boundary work done by the air, in kJ (work by the system positive).
questions.explanation: For an isothermal ideal gas W = mRT ln(V2/V1) = 0.20 x 0.287 x 300 x ln(1/3) = -18.92 kJ. The value is negative because the volume decreases, so the surroundings do work on the air.

questions.stem: A gas at 100 kPa and 0.60 m$^3$ is compressed along $pV^{1.25}=\text{constant}$ until the pressure reaches 400 kPa. Find the boundary work done by the gas in kJ (work by the system positive).
questions.explanation: First V2 = V1 (p1/p2)^(1/n) = 0.60 x (0.25)^0.8 = 0.1979 m^3. Then W = (p2V2 - p1V1)/(1 - n) = (79.17 - 60.0)/(-0.25) = -76.68 kJ, negative because the gas is compressed.

questions.stem: Starting from the definition of boundary work, derive the work done by an ideal gas expanding isothermally from volume $V_1$ to $V_2$ at temperature $T$, and state the sign for expansion and compression.
markingGuide: Starts from W = integral of p dV along the path
Uses pV = mRT with T constant to write p = mRT/V
Integrates to obtain mRT ln(V2/V1), equivalently p1V1 ln(V2/V1)
States positive for V2 > V1 (expansion) and negative for V2 < V1 under the stated convention
Mentions the assumption of a quasi-equilibrium process and ideal gas behaviour
questions.explanation: Substituting p = mRT/V into the integral gives mRT times the integral of dV/V, which is mRT ln(V2/V1). The sign follows the logarithm, so expansion is positive and compression negative.

questions.stem: A gas can be taken between the same two end states on a p-V diagram along two different paths. Explain with reference to the area under each path why the boundary work differs, and say what that implies about work as a quantity.
markingGuide: Boundary work equals the area under the path on a p-V diagram
Different paths between the same states enclose different areas
So work depends on the path, not just on the end states
Work is therefore not a property of the system and is not a state function
Identifies an increment of work as an inexact differential, or says it is energy in transit across the boundary
questions.explanation: Because the integral of p dV needs the pressure at each volume along the way, two routes with different pressure histories give different areas. This is why work is described as a path function and is not a property of a state.
